summary: German greetings follow two questions: what time is it, and do I say du or Sie to this person? With Sie-people you use the full formulas – Guten Tag, Auf Wiedersehen, Wie geht es Ihnen? – with du-people the short ones – Hallo, Tschüss, Wie geht’s? / Wie geht es dir?. The formulas do not change for a man or a woman (unlike Arabic and Hebrew), but they change by region: Grüß Gott and Servus in the south and Austria, Moin in the north, Grüezi in Switzerland. Guten Tag / Morgen / Abend are accusatives (einen guten Tag wünschen), gute Nacht is feminine.

blocks.title: Gute Nacht is not hello
blocks.text: You arrive at 11 p.m. with Guten Abend; Gute Nacht is only for going to bed or parting late.

blocks.title: Regional greetings
blocks.text: Grüß Gott (Bavaria, Austria: polite hello), Servus (south and Austria: hi and bye among friends), Moin (north: hello at any hour), Grüezi (Switzerland: polite hello), Ade (Swabia: bye).

blocks.title: Bitte does two jobs
blocks.text: bitte = please (Ein Glas Wasser, bitte) and you’re welcome (Danke! – Bitte!).

askYourself: Do I say du or Sie to this person? (stranger, adult, office → Sie; friend, family, child, peer → du)
What time is it: morning, day, evening, bedtime?
Am I arriving or leaving? Is it a phone call (Auf Wiederhören)?
Where am I? South: Grüß Gott; north: Moin; Switzerland: Grüezi.
Small slip or real regret? Entschuldigung for a bump or to get attention; Es tut mir leid for regret and sympathy.
Someone offers something: do I want it (Ja, bitte!) or not (Nein, danke!)?
steps: Choose the formula for the moment.
Answer in kind: Gut, danke – und dir? / und Ihnen?

traps: Gute Nacht is never a greeting on arrival.
A bare Danke! when someone offers you something often means “no, thanks”.
Wie geht es Ihnen? with a capital I; ihnen (small i) = them.

guten Tag, not *gute Tag: Tag, Morgen and Abend are masculine accusatives.

Only Nacht is feminine (gute Nacht).
Wie geht’s? expects a short real answer (Gut, danke – und dir?), not the same question back.

seeAlso.note: Arabic answers a greeting in kind (as-salāmu ʿalaykum – wa-ʿalaykumu s-salām) and many formulas change for a man, a woman or a group.

Hebrew shalom is hello and goodbye.

“how are you” changes for a man or a woman (ma shlomkha? / ma shlomekh?).
Chinese 你好 / 您好 (polite), 再见, 谢谢 – 不客气: politeness by choosing 您, no gender.
du, ihr and Sie: the same choice decides the greeting.

notes.text:
- Γεια σου / Γεια σας split like du / Sie.
- Καλημέρα, Καλησπέρα, Καληνύχτα are like Guten Morgen, Guten Abend, Gute Nacht.
- But γεια is hello and goodbye; German splits Hallo and Tschüss.

- Привет / Здравствуйте follow the ты / вы line just as Hallo / Guten Tag follow du / Sie.
- Спокойной ночи, like Gute Nacht, is only for parting at night.

Buenas noches greets on arrival in the evening too; **Gute Nacht never does** – arriving at night you say Guten Abend.

Hola / Buenos días follow the same tú / usted logic as Hallo / Guten Tag.

Wie geht’s? expects a short real answer, not the same question back as “How are you?” often does:
→ Gut, danke – und dir?

Gute Nacht, like “Good night”, is only for parting.

Bonjour / Salut, Bonsoir, Bonne nuit (only for bedtime) and tu / vous work much like Guten Tag / Hallo, Guten Abend, Gute Nacht and du / Sie.

Ça va ? is Wie geht’s?

- salām works at any hour and xodāhāfez says goodbye; German has a formula for each part of the day.
- The du / Sie choice matches tu / šomā.
namaskār works at any hour; German changes the greeting with the time of day and with du / Sie.

Arabic greetings come with a fixed reply (as-salāmu ʿalaykum – wa-ʿalaykum as-salām; ṣabāḥ al-khayr – ṣabāḥ an-nūr) and change for a man or a woman (kayfa ḥāluka / ḥāluki).

German formulas are the same for everyone, and the answer is free:
→ Guten Morgen! – Morgen!

- shalom is hello and goodbye; German has Hallo and Tschüss.
- ma shlomkha / ma shlomekh change for a man or a woman; Wie geht es dir? / Ihnen? change only for du / Sie.

- Merhaba, Günaydın, İyi akşamlar and İyi geceler (only for parting at night) work like Hallo, Guten Morgen, Guten Abend and Gute Nacht.
- Nasılsın? / Nasılsınız? mirror Wie geht es dir? / Ihnen?

Ohayō (gozaimasu) / Konnichiwa / Konbanwa change with the time of day, as German greetings do.

But politeness is shown in the form (ohayō vs ohayō gozaimasu); German shows it with du / Sie (Wie geht es dir? / Ihnen?).

annyeonghaseyo serves at any hour, and its politeness is in the ending (annyeong among friends).

German Hallo / Guten Tag differ the same way, but the greeting also changes with the time of day.

Swahili greets by age and respect (Shikamoo to elders, answered Marahaba) and asks Habari? – Nzuri.

German respect is the pronoun Sie, chosen for strangers of any age, not only for elders.

- 你好 / 您好 split like Hallo – Guten Tag / du – Sie.
- 晚安 is only for bedtime, like Gute Nacht.
- 再见 (“again see”) has the same image as Auf Wiedersehen.

Xin chào is followed by the kinship word for the person (chào anh, chào bác).

German greetings name no one and choose only between du and Sie.

Inuktitut has no polite “you”; **German must choose du or Sie** before the first sentence (Wie geht es dir? / Ihnen?).

danke is the everyday word for qujannamiik.

- Ciao / Buongiorno and tu / Lei split like Hallo / Guten Tag and du / Sie.
- Buonanotte, like Gute Nacht, is only for parting late.
- But ciao is hello and bye, where German splits Hallo and Tschüss.
- Arrivederci has the image of Auf Wiedersehen (“until we see again”).

- Mirëmëngjes, Mirëdita, Mirëmbrëma, Natën e mirë match Guten Morgen, Guten Tag, Guten Abend, Gute Nacht.
- Mirupafshim (“may we see each other well”) has the image of Auf Wiedersehen.
- Si jeni? / Si je? split like Wie geht es Ihnen? / Wie geht’s?

Boa noite greets on arrival in the evening too; **Gute Nacht never does** – say Guten Abend.

- Olá / Bom dia and tu / o senhor follow the logic of Hallo / Guten Tag and du / Sie.
- Where obrigado / obrigada changes with the speaker, Danke never does.

If politeness lives in verb endings in your language, in German it lives in the choice of du or Sie and of the formula:
→ Wie geht es Ihnen? (Sie) – Wie geht’s? (du)
→ Guten Tag (Sie) – Hallo (du)

If your greetings have a plain and a polite form, German splits the same way (Hallo / Guten Tag, Wie geht’s? / Wie geht es Ihnen?).

It adds the time of day: Guten Morgen, Guten Abend, and Gute Nacht only at bedtime.

- If your greeting changes with the sex of the person you speak to, German does not: Wie geht es dir? to a man or a woman – only du / Sie and the time of day change the formula.
- If one word of yours is both hello and goodbye, German splits it: Hallo / Guten Tag – Tschüss / Auf Wiedersehen.
